summary: Technical deep dive focused on sizing reserved GPU pools and burst policies. Reviewed queueing models, KV cache warmup, batching tradeoffs and hybrid VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a 24h stochastic simulation, deliver pricing, and follow up on network topology for Private deployment.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, uh thanks for carving out time. Jordan from Redwood here, I'm the AE on this account. Priya is our systems SE, Liam is on for a few minutes too. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Miguel Alvarez: Good, thanks. Busy, but excited to walk through capacity planning, this is the big one for us.
[00:12] Rina Cho: Hi all. Quick note, we care about tail latency more than average, 95th must stay under 180ms for realtime fraud checks.
[00:18] Priya Natarajan: Thanks Rina, we'll anchor sizing on 95/99 pctl. A quick agenda: 1) clarify production traffic shape, 2) discuss queueing model + burst policy options, 3) reserved GPU sizing and warmup strategies, 4) VPC/on-prem implications.
[00:30] Alexei Volkov: Also want to understand quantization impact — we currently run a distilled 7B for embeddings and a 34B for conversation.
[00:36] Jordan Lee: Noted. Miguel, can you confirm peak qps and percent of long runs vs short token paths?
[00:41] Miguel Alvarez: Sure. Baseline online qps is about 120 rps for fraud scoring, spiking up to 1,800 rps in promo windows; typical sequence len ranges 8-80 tokens, median 22, tail lots of one-offs at 200-400 tokens for transcripts.
[00:56] Priya Natarajan: Okay that's helpful. So we have heavy burstiness — classic candidate for reserved pools + burst queues. Two immediate levers: prewarmed pools (reserved GPUs) for steady-state and an ephemeral burst queue that can either use pooled GPUs or fall back to lower-cost quantized variants.
[01:13] Rina Cho: On the fall back — how deterministic is the model variant routing? We can't have sudden hallucination or inconsistent outputs in fraud scoring.
[01:20] Priya Natarajan: Right. We recommend policy-based routing: prefer exact model match for high-confidence routes (fraud SLOs) and route non-critical paths to quantized or smaller models. We can define per-route SLAs in the Console.
[01:32] Miguel Alvarez: Can you explain the queueing math — you mentioned Erlang earlier, is that what you use?
[01:38] Priya Natarajan: Yeah we typically model using an M/M/c approximation for warm pools but for bursty traffic we use an Erlang-C formulation to estimate waiting probability under finite servers and admission control. In practice we run stochastic sims because arrival process is not Poisson — it's highly correlated with events and marketing bursts.
[01:53] Liam O'Connor: Just to add, we instrument prefix hits vs full KV cache misses. Warmed KV cache can drop service time by up to 30-40% on long sequences because attention KV lookups avoid recomputing prefix. So warmup matters a lot.
[02:07] Alexei Volkov: How do you simulate KV warmup? We saw big variance with cold clients.
[02:12] Priya Natarajan: We replay traces and simulate cache warmup by modeling per-client prefix reuse and global prefix frequency. For enterprise customers we can ingest real histograms and run a 24h replay that includes diurnal and spike events. That will tell us prewarm fraction needed to hit 95th latency target.
[02:28] Rina Cho: What's the recommended prewarm ratio for our shape?
[02:31] Priya Natarajan: Ballpark for your traffic I'd start with 60-70% prewarm on reserved pools and allow burst queue to use ephemeral quantized instances for the remainder. But we need the sim to be sure. It's an empirical number.
[02:42] Miguel Alvarez: And cost? We want to avoid overprovisioning monthly committed spend.
[02:46] Jordan Lee: We'll provide a pricing matrix. Typical commit tiers give 20-40% discount vs on-demand; plus burst egress is billed separately. For some customers a hybrid reservation with autoscaling headroom is cheaper than a large flat reserved pool.
[02:58] Alexei Volkov: We have a VPC deployment plan; data residency is strict — can Redwood Dedicated run in our VPC or do we need Private on-prem?
[03:07] Priya Natarajan: Redwood Dedicated supports customer VPC peering and Private mode can be either a VPC-controlled control plane or fully on-prem. The difference is where the control plane sits and the network egress path. For throughput-limited workloads we usually prefer Dedicated in your cloud region with peering to avoid egress hops.
[03:22] Sophie Mills: If we do Dedicated + burst to public region, are logs and inference payloads ever routed outside our VPC?
[03:29] Jordan Lee: By default telemetry metadata goes to Redwood analytics but for Private deployments we can push logs into your Kinesis/SQS or S3 + KMS so you retain custody. We can detail that in the security pack.
[03:40] Miguel Alvarez: Back to queueing — what's the behavior when reserved pools saturate? Do you reject or queue?
[03:46] Priya Natarajan: We support configurable admission control: queue depth limits, prioritized routes, and automatic fallback to secondary model variants. If queueing would violate latency SLO we can short-circuit and return a degraded result or fail-fast depending on policy.
[03:58] Rina Cho: Hmm we prefer fail-fast with a clear status code so upstream can handle it, rather than degraded model that might miss fraud signals.
[04:04] Priya Natarajan: That's straightforward — set the policy to reject when estimated wait > 120ms. We'll demo that in the sim.
[04:10] Liam O'Connor: Also worth noting that batching windows heavily influence tail latency. If you set a batching window of 10-20ms you can amortize kernel overhead but you'll add batching latency. For your SLOs, batch windows should be short — 4-8ms maybe — but then throughput per-GPU drops.
[04:28] Miguel Alvarez: We can tolerate some batching, but not at the cost of false negatives.
[04:32] Priya Natarajan: Understood. We'll run sims across batch window values and quantization levels: FP16, int8, int4. Quantization reduces memory footprint and allows more concurrent streams per GPU but can change model behavior. For fraud detection we recommend quantization only after validation on your eval set.
[04:50] Alexei Volkov: Have you seen int4 degrade scores materially for classification tasks?
[04:54] Priya Natarajan: We have seen some drift in int4 for certain LLMs on out-of-distribution prompts. Usually retraining or a small calibration layer mitigates it. That's why we tie quality monitoring to prompt sets — Redwood Optimize will alert regression.
[05:09] Miguel Alvarez: Good; include that in the deliverable. We need clear pass/fail criteria for quantized variants.
[05:15] Jordan Lee: We'll include a QA matrix. Quick pause — any questions on networking for Private?
[05:20] Rina Cho: Two items: egress costs and DNS routing. If bursts spill over into public clouds, will load balancers introduce jitter?
[05:28] Priya Natarajan: Minimal if peered correctly; jitter mostly from cross-region hops. Our advice: keep reserved capacity in the same AZs where traffic originates and configure affinity. For ingress we support SNI-routing and TLS termination in your VPC.
[05:40] Miguel Alvarez: Let's walk through an example sim — like a 3hr promo where qps ramps 10x.
[05:45] Priya Natarajan: Yeah I'll narrate: simulation assumptions: 3 reserved GPUs in region A, each can handle X concurrent streams for your 34B model at FP16, baseline traffic Poisson with event-driven spikes. We run Erlang-C to compute P(wait) and tail wait. Then run stochastic replay of actual trace to model cache warmup and observed tail latencies.
[06:05] Liam O'Connor: In practice we also inject network variance and backend datastore latencies because those add to tail.
[06:11] Alexei Volkov: Do you model queueing per-GPU or per-pool?
[06:15] Priya Natarajan: Per-pool with sharding heuristics: routes can be pinned to GPU subsets to preserve KV cache locality. Pinned shards help warmup but reduce statistical multiplexing. There's a trade off between cache hit-rate and utilization.
[06:29] Miguel Alvarez: That tradeoff seems central — do you have any heuristics?
[06:33] Priya Natarajan: Yes: if you have high prefix reuse among clients, pinning improves 95th latency significantly. If reuse is low, prefer pooling to maximize throughput. We can compute an optimal pin fraction.
[06:45] Rina Cho: Are there autoscaling knobs we can tune in Dedicated?
[06:49] Jordan Lee: Autoscaling supports scale-up cooldowns, scale-to-zero for ephemeral pools, and burst headroom. For Reserved pools we recommend scale-up cooldowns of ~2-5 minutes to avoid oscillation, plus a short prewarm trigger that starts warming KV caches when an alert threshold is crossed.
[07:03] Miguel Alvarez: Prewarm trigger — how fast can KV warmup realistically happen?
[07:07] Priya Natarajan: Depends on prefix reuse. For highly-reused prefixes, warmup is minutes; for unique prefixes it's hours, because you need many requests to populate. That's why we pre-warm common prefixes from logs where possible.
[07:21] Sophie Mills: How do you pre-warm without replaying PII data?
[07:24] Priya Natarajan: We support anonymized replay or synthetic prefix construction. We never persist sensitive payloads in the prewarm pipeline; it's just token prefixes used to fill KV entries. All storage can be KMS-encrypted.
[07:36] Miguel Alvarez: Okay, what about fallback policies — is there a hybrid where we burst to a different model family in another region? Latency might increase though.
[07:44] Priya Natarajan: Yes policy-based routing supports cross-region fallback to a compatible model variant; we rank fallbacks by cost and latency penalty. For critical routes you can disable cross-region fallback.
[07:55] Alexei Volkov: Let's talk numbers — if we wanted a 99th < 300ms target during nominal load (120 rps) and survive a 15x burst with 99th < 500ms, what does that look like?
[08:04] Priya Natarajan: Preliminary: you'd need a reserved baseline sized for nominal plus an autoscale headroom that can add ~8-12 GPUs quickly, or a smaller baseline with a larger burst quota to ephemeral pools. Exact # depends on quantization and batch window. We'll produce scenarios.
[08:20] Miguel Alvarez: Can the simulation output costs side-by-side (tokens, GPU-hours, egress)?
[08:24] Jordan Lee: Yes we output tokenized cost, GPU-hour cost, and an estimate for egress. We'll also show cost per model-call at p50/p95 for each scenario.
[08:33] Rina Cho: For reporting — can we get an SLA attachment that maps to our error codes and expected fallback behaviors?
[08:38] Jordan Lee: Absolutely — part of the Reserved proposal includes a runbook mapping error codes, retry behavior, and alerts.
[08:44] Miguel Alvarez: One more: what monitoring hooks are available for KV cache?
[08:48] Liam O'Connor: We export metrics: kv_cache_hit_rate, kv_cache_load_latency, avg_prefix_age, per-shard utilization. There are tracing spans that show per-token latency broken into kernel compute, kv-lookup, and network egress.
[09:02] Alexei Volkov: Great. Anything else?
[09:05] Sophie Mills: Could you include a worked example that shows cost per spike (e.g., promo of 4 hours) vs committed cost?
[09:11] Jordan Lee: Yep, we'll include a worked promo example and a sensitivity analysis.
[09:15] Miguel Alvarez: Ok let's outline deliverables and deadlines.
[09:18] Priya Natarajan: Deliverables: 1) 24h stochastic sim (Priya) w/ PDF and recommended reserved pool config, 2) Pricing tiers + contract language (Jordan), 3) VPC/Private whiteboard and network runbook draft (Jordan + Rina), 4) QA matrix for quantization (Priya + Alexei).
[09:35] Rina Cho: We will upload traces and histograms by EOD tomorrow.
[09:39] Jordan Lee: Perfect — once we get the traces Priya will run the sim and we aim to have results by 2026-06-20.
[09:46] Miguel Alvarez: Thx, this was useful. Quick note on the simulation — please include an Erlang-C and a replay-based model so we can see differences.
[09:54] Priya Natarajan: Will do, Miguel. We'll show the M/M/c/Erlang-C approximations and the replay overlay.
[09:59] Jordan Lee: Ok closing notes — next call tentatively 2026-06-22 to review sim results. Thanks everyone.
[10:06] Sophie Mills: Thanks all.
[10:08] End of recording (62:00)
